articles.description: Congo Halts Cobalt Exports As Price Collapse Fuels Resource Nationalism The Democratic Republic of Congo is using its dominance in cobalt production to restrict exports in an interventionist move to reverse the collapse in global prices. Bloomberg reports that ARECOMS, the country's strategic minerals regulator, has imposed a ban on cobalt exports that will take effect at the end of November to combat plunging prices for the metal, which is widely used in EV batteries. ARECOMS said the decision is intended " to address the oversupply in the international market and to promote a sustainable rebalancing of the market ." The decision marks Congo's second export ban since February 2025 ( read here ), and it  exemplifies the use of resource nationalism to influence global cobalt prices . This theme is becoming all too familiar and is growing worldwide.  The first suspension lasted eight months before being replaced by quotas that restricted shipments to less than half the country's 2024 output. articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
articles.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. articles.title: After Eight: the story of Satpal Ram - documentary
articles.description: It is 40 years since a racially charged attack at a curry house led to Satpal Ram’s conviction for murder, but today Britain’s post-pub curry culture still has a dark side. Ram spent 24 years in prison before a global campaign for justice, led by bands including Asian Dub Foundation and Primal Scream, secured his release from prison. His case raises crucial questions about the UK’s ongoing struggle for racial equality Continue reading...

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone

articles.title: ‘The place becomes a jewellery box of glittering lights’: readers’ favourite winter city breaks in Europe
articles.description: Ice-skating, illuminated medieval buildings and seasonal treats feature in your picks of atmospheric winter cities • Tell us about a winter weekend break – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher In December, Antwerp is transformed into a jewellery box of glittering lights. Christmas markets throng the historic squares, and the illuminated facades of the gothic and Renaissance buildings create a magical atmosphere. At Groenplaats, we watched ice-skaters circle the statue of Rubens, while at Handschoenmarkt we listened to carols courtesy of the Singing Christmas Tree. There’s plenty to do during the daytime, too: we admired the art nouveau architecture in Zurenborg and paid homage to Bruegel’s Dull Gret at Museum Mayer van den Bergh . The famous brown cafes make the perfect place for a cosy nightcap. Emily Continue reading...

articles.title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?
articles.description: Experts say seaweed could be a solution in the fight against global plastic waste, which doubled between 2000 and 2019 The name of the Northamptonshire hamlet of Nobottle means “new building” in Old English. But on a Tuesday last month, the name of the tiny cluster of houses in the East Midlands took on a whole different meaning. Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. The drinks were in edible pods as part of a pilot project with Notpla, a company that makes biodegradable packaging. Roughly half of the 30 or so local residents tried the product lined up on trays. Continue reading...

articles.title: In a flap: how the butterfly became a symbol of gen Z resilience – and anxiety
articles.description: The delicate insect has become fashion’s favourite motif again – but having represented sexuality in the 90s and the soul in Greco-Roman times, what does it say about youth culture today? • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In the new Gucci campaign, Mariah Carey blows a goodbye kiss to 2026 in the most Mariahhhh way possible. Dressed in a fake fur coat and an azure dress, she enters a Christmas party to the twinkly sounds of All I Want For Christmas Is You. There are beautiful people, presents wrapped with Gucci string and butterflies, which have been associated with the popstar since her 1997 album, Butterfly, but have recently fluttered back to become a symbol of gen Z defiance and girlhood. Carey serves as fairy godmother to the other “pop girlies” who have embraced the emblem, from PinkPantheress to Dua Lipa; Rachel Chinouriri to Marina and the Diamonds. At the Academy Museum gala in October, the singer Janelle Monáe looked as if she might take flight in a Robert Wun couture gown, with wide, yonic wings. articles.title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’ Described as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting. While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida . GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments. Continue reading...

articles.title: Consent under scrutiny: where does youth end and adulthood begin?
articles.description: After the Brand and Walliams revelations, calls for a ‘staggered’ age of consent are redefining what makes someone ‘adult’ The fact that the age of sexual consent in Britain is set at 16 is thanks to a chimney sweep’s daughter from Marylebone, London, called Eliza Armstrong – not that she had any say in the matter. In June 1885, Armstrong had just turned 13 when she was sold for sex by her alcoholic mother for the sum of £5. She believed she was going to work as a gentleman’s maid; instead, the child was taken to a brothel, where she was examined to prove she was a virgin and drugged with chloroform to await the gentleman who had “purchased” her virginity. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guide #270: Grand Theft Auto VI is everywhere – but is it really the cultural event of the decade?
articles.description: In this week’s newsletter: It could be the biggest entertainment release ever, but its reach reveals the limit of shared cultural experience An estimated cost of $1bn. A development period of 13 years. A production team of 5,000 people. A game map the size of Manchester. An estimated 24m copies sold through pre-orders and launch day alone, generating $2.36bn. Thousands upon thousands of days of leave booked and sick days taken to play the thing, costing the US economy an estimated $1bn (yep, another billion figure) in lost productivity. The scale of Grand Theft Auto VI – and the tidal wave of facts and figures surrounding its making and economic impact – truly boggles the mind. Even if you, like me, are unlikely to ever sit down and play the thing, you will struggle to escape its influence. Footage both sinister and benign – from graphic shooting sprees to mellow clips of its protagonists strolling, hand in hand, down the beach – will follow you around Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok. Whatever your preferred publication, left or right, high- or lowbrow, it will have proffered its own take on the game, whether it’s to bemoan its godless influence on adolescent men or to laud its u

articles.title: Why I love Stockholm in winter: ‘A return to slowing down, cosying up and revering every glimmer of light’
articles.description: Swedes adore the festive season, embracing the shorter days with fairy lights, yuletide feasts and fun in the snow I’ll let you in on a secret: I often tell people that summer is the best time to visit Stockholm. Clouds drift across impossibly blue skies, we skip around midsummer maypoles singing folk songs and cruise the waterways, bobbing and weaving through the archipelago’s 30,000-plus islands. That’s mostly because I want to keep December in Stockholm to myself. Soft white snow dusts buildings of ochre and burnt sienna like icing on a cake. Festive candles light up pavements leading to cosy cafes, where the earthy, buttery smell of seasonal saffron buns ( lussekatter ) replaces cinnamon buns for fika , our revered tradition of coffee and cake. Continue reading...

articles.title: Dress for the dancefloor – and go big on jewellery: 51 ways to look fabulous this party season
articles.description: Whether it’s styling tricks that cost nothing or chic festive finds, our fashion expert takes the stress out of getting ready • The best women’s coats Oh look, how lovely – a party invitation. That’s nice of them, isn’t it? How exciting. Haven’t seen the whatsits since, ooh, last Christmas, I suppose. Mmm, hope they have mince pies. Can’t wait! Fast forward to the night itself and you have spent 45 minutes trying on tops in front of the bedroom mirror. Too dressy? Not dressy enough? Should I have got my nails done? Will everyone else be in jeans? Are sequins too much? Maybe we should just stay in and watch the last episode of Black Doves? Continue reading...

articles.title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?
articles.description: After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11 . Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage . She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California. Continue reading...

articles.title: Unreal deals: the scam websites targeting Black Friday bargain hunters
articles.description: AI is being used to clone retailers’ sites and ‘poison’ chatbots into recommending them, experts say Black Friday is coming so you search online for the coat you have been after in the hope you can get it at a good price. Within a few minutes, you find just the right one, in the colour you want and at a huge discount. You decide to take advantage of the bargain quickly and transfer the money then wait for it to be delivered. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cassette, London WC2: ‘One of the greatest dishes I’ve eaten all year’ – restaurant review | Grace Dent on restaurants
articles.description: A discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the deadly bloody serious I booked my lunch table at Cassette , a new French restaurant in Covent Garden, central London, while watching a viral video of a blasé Parisian couple , mid-riot, sipping wine and smoking Gauloises near the Arc de Triomphe. Yes, fiery flames of mass anarchy, but also, yes, finishing one’s glass is important, too. The Brits keep opening Parisian-style restaurants as a quiet admission that these people are really bloody cool, and this new one from Mark Gurney and Matt Bushnell , the pair behind Peckham’s Levan (also very cool, incidentally), serves the likes of a coq au vin jaune pie with a chicken leg saluting from its crust, and panisse with chopped mussels and green tomato. There’s also pork chop with sauce Talleyrand, Maldon oysters with beurre blanc, and a cocktail called Jet Fuel that combines Get 27 , the green mint liqueur that gives every Parisian a starry-eyed memory of their parents’ dinner parties, with calvados and coffee liqueur. Cassette is a discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the actually deadly bloody serious. Yes, dress up fancy, if you wish, but you can also slide in her

articles.description: Empty nesters Anna and Richard have found the freedom and space to experiment with intimacy • How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously I’m a much more active participant sexually now. I used to be more reactive Continue reading...

articles.title: Why I love Madrid in winter: ‘Locals get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats’
articles.description: The streets and squares of the Spanish capital come alive with Madrileños shopping, drinking and dining outdoors, warmed by lap blankets and patio heaters Live in Madrid long enough and you hear the same weather-related proverbs again and again. One old saying goes that the seasons in the Spanish capital break down to “nine months of winter and three months of hell”. And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle. Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. Many local people get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats,

articles.title: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause
articles.description: Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con? ‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live , billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee. The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. ( Fungi are big news in the me

articles.title: The footballer-turned-BookTuber who made an obscure Tolstoy novella a belated bestseller
articles.description: Once named the best player in Brazil, Gustavo Scarpa’s literature obsession has inspired thousands to become bookworms Julián Scatolaro noticed something odd was occurring when several people came into his bookshop over the space of a few days, all asking for Leo Tolstoy’s novella The Death of Ivan Ilyich . The 35-year-old, who owns a bookshop in the small Argentine city of Chajarí, 311 miles from Buenos Aires, said the sudden interest in a book written in 1886 was surprising enough. But this was particularly strange because when his customers ask for works by the Russian writer, they usually want War and Peace . In a video he posted about the mystery, he called it the “ Tolstoy enigma ”. Continue reading...

articles.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
articles.description: Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it? Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill? Con

articles.title: How to make nasi goreng – recipe | Felicity Cloake's Masterclass
articles.description: The richly flavoured Indonesian and Malaysian fried-rice dish is quick to cook, but calls for a little groundwork. Here’s how to make it Unless you’ve had the admirable foresight to prepare the spice paste in advance, thus turning this into just a quick assembly job, nasi goreng is not a fried rice that you whip up in five minutes from last night’s leftovers. Neither, however, is it particularly complex, and the richly savoury, shallot-sweet base gives it a depth of flavour that more than justifies the modest investment of time. Prep 25 min Chill 2 hr+ Cook 5 min Serves 2 Continue reading...

articles.title: Interpol and Bloc Party review – two of 00s indie’s most revered acts go toe-to-toe
articles.description: Utilita Arena Cardiff Kele Okereke has a tough challenge selling Bloc Party’s trite latest album – a far cry from Interpol’s ‘masterpiece’ eighth record, performed here to darkly hypnotic effect Try as one might to resist comparison, the balance of this particular yin and yang has been shifting for some time. Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era. Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners. Continue reading...

articles.title: Nine Night is back and proves itself a modern classic full of secrets, squabbles and laughs
articles.description: Kiln theatre, London Exquisitely acted, and directed with lightness and depth, Natasha Gordon’s 2018 tragicomedy about a Jamaican matriarch’s wake is moving and never mawkish The death of a parent has a way of blowing up the lives of family members it leaves behind. The combustions of grief, greed and secrets revealed around a barely buried coffin litter the tragicomic works of playwrights such as Tracy Letts (August: Osage County) and Branden Jacobs-Jenkins (Appropriate). You might want to add Natasha Gordon’s debut play to that canon, although it comes wrapped in its own distinct cultural tradition. Its structure revolves around the Caribbean funeral ritual that commemorates the death of a loved one over nine nights. A debut play written by a young Black British woman, featuring an almost entirely Black British cast, it got a huge reaction at the National Theatre in 2018 . Continue reading...

articles.title: Hark! Errollyn Wallen’s glittering nativity opera A Christmas Miracle is a credit to Britten’s community vision
articles.description: Orford church, Suffolk Performed in the venue where Noye’s Fludde premiered and based on the same text, this festive new work shines with exuberant young performers, distinctive singalongs, lustrous designs and the spirit of mucking in When Benjamin Britten wrote Noye’s Fludde, he essentially invented community opera. Bringing professionals together with enthusiastic local amateurs, everyone mucking in to play, sing and make sets and costumes, isn’t only great fun; done right, it fosters a love of music-making that can last a lifetime. Such projects, the composer declared with his best socialist hat on, created works that were “useful to the living”. For decades, Britten contemplated a nativity opera, which somehow never transpired. Now, Errollyn Wallen , Master of the King’s Music, has filled the gap. A Christmas Miracle, co-produced by Mahogany Opera and Britten Pears Arts, sets texts from the same Chester mystery plays that inspired Noye’s Fludde, and premiered in the Orford church that Britten chose in 1958. Continue reading...

articles.title: Kindness of strangers: I was stuck sitting in a sea of legs and feet when a beautiful young man offered me his hand
articles.description: This young man took the time to notice the middle-aged woman sitting in the dust and didn’t just walk past. He reached out Read more in the kindness of strangers series My knees aren’t in terribly good condition. I’m at that age. A few years ago, I was at a big hippy festival out in the Australian desert near Deniliquin. There, I attended a talk and was sitting down on the ground at the rear of a large group of people listening to a speaker. When the talk finished, everybody got up to leave, streaming past me as they went. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sounds may seem louder or even painful as you age. Here’s why
articles.description: For some, everyday loud noise becomes bothersome. Researchers call this sound hypersensitivity and it’s worth knowing whether it’s due to ageing or not Loud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. If that’s you, it’s worth knowing what’s due to normal ageing and what isn’t. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cat’s whiskers: Nan Goldin proves that she’s the greatest US artist since Warhol – review
articles.description: Hayward Gallery, London The photographer finds echoes of Caravaggio and Greek myth in her erotic images, while her disturbing animal montages show that while humans can be beautiful, we are far from innocent It’s the dirty realism of Nan Goldin ’s images, her unfazed photography of the rough seams of spontaneous, dangerous lives, that enables her to create a film of such unlikely ambition as Stendhal Syndrome. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen. She infects you with it in a ravishing work housed in what looks like a bronze yurt entered via a vaulted corridor. If this seems ostentatious, the film justifies the ceremony. A montage of sensual images teems with Goldin’s uniquely raw, immediate feel for the human presence as she photographs her friends, mostly in the nude, legs wrapped round each other, or lying in a swoon, or touching thems

articles.title: ‘A Nintendo Switch – yes, I know I’m 67’: the best gifts for every generation, picked by real people aged 2 to 103
articles.description: We asked everyone from gen Alpha preschoolers to retired boomers, celebs and Guardian writers what’s on their gift list this year – here’s what they said • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 How old are you, and what would you like for Christmas? That’s normally a question reserved for children visiting Santa’s grotto, but it’s one we put to hundreds of you of all ages to see what different generations have on their gift lists. The results may just help you hone your approach to present buying across generations this Christmas, or at least offer an insight into the tastes of each group. But be warned: from the boomer who wants a Nintendo Switch to the 30-somethings collecting vinyl and brewing craft beer, some answers might surprise you. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson
articles.description: He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US. Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘What if joining the resistance got your friends executed?’ The chilling new films casting Nazi collaborators in a fresh light
articles.description: For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light? A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown , which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched. The trauma of wartime violence only comes rushing back in occasional bursts: blurry flashbacks show shadowy figures pointing guns at temples and bodies thudding to the floor. But the red fabric billowing through the fog of her memory is not the Nazi flag but liberated Denmark’s white-crossed Dannebrog . The black-clad executioners are not SS officers but resistance fighters reckoning with colla

articles.title: ‘Once installed, there’s no getting rid of it’: what Falklands oil plans mean for its seals, whales and penguins
articles.description: While Argentina and the UK dispute sovereignty over the islands and its vast oil reserves, environmentalists fear for one of the Atlantic’s richest ecosystems From the air, the main Falkland Islands form two large, jagged shapes against the South Atlantic. East Falkland and West Falkland are surrounded by 778 smaller islands and islets east of Patagonia’s southern tip. The archipelago, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, is home to large colonies of albatrosses and penguins. Its waters, with those of the Patagonian shelf, provide feeding grounds for sea lions, southern elephant seals and southern right whales. Continue reading...

articles.title: Undoing Brexit is the right thing to attempt – but sadly, I can't see Andy Burnham pulling it off | Paul Taylor
articles.description: Brussels rolled out a warm welcome for the PM but toxic UK politics around rejoining have not gone away Despite the beaming smiles and the symbolic triple handshake, the summit intended to reset the UK’s tortured relationship with the EU showed just how difficult undoing Brexit will be a decade after Britons voted to leave. To be sure, Brussels laid on a warm welcome. Andy Burnham’s first summit with the heads of the EU institutions felt like the homecoming of an old friend who had been away too long, rather than a meeting to settle some awkward leftovers of a bitter divorce. Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre Continue reading...

articles.title: The truth about dying: hospice workers on what loved ones should know
articles.description: Anna Gordon met hospice care workers across the UK, learning how dignity and choice help create meaningful moments for patients Most people in the UK actively avoid conversations about death and dying. They can be visibly uncomfortable when you raise the subject. When people try to talk about it, it tends to be euphemistically. This is a mistake, one that can stop you from making important choices for yourself or your loved ones. It can increase fear and misunderstanding about what death can look like, while open conversations can help to ease these feelings and bring a sense of calm, peace and, on occasion, even beauty to the event. Jenna Heritage: ‘Everyone’s big fear is that they are going to die in pain’ Continue reading...

articles.title: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find
articles.description: Scientific and satellite findings warn of widespread contamination in Gaza, posing grave threats to public health ‘for generations to come’ Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report. Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come. Continue reading...

articles.title: MPs urge Miliband to force UK overseas territories to publish public company registers
articles.description: Improvements in corporate transparency ‘essential’ amid ‘outright disregard for the will of parliament’, says cross-party group Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a decade after parliament voted for transparency. Ahead of a meeting between the foreign secretary and overseas territories this week, a cross-party group of MPs from Labour, the Tories, Lib Dems and Greens wrote to Miliband calling on him to mandate public registers of beneficial ownership of companies. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cost of renting in Britain to rise twice as fast as buying amid shortage of properties
articles.description: Rents to rise by 14% until at least 2029, Hamptons predicts, as high demand for properties and low supply push up costs for tenants The cost of renting a home in Britain is expected to rise about twice as fast as that of buying one until at least 2029, according to research, with shrinking supply pushing up the prices paid by tenants. Rents on newly agreed lets are forecast to grow by 14.2% between 2026 and 2029, compared with house price growth of 7.2%, according to forecasts from estate agent Hamptons. Continue reading...

articles.title: Fewer than half in UK will pay TV licence fee within a decade, report warns
articles.description: Analysis for thinktank points to cycle of falling income leading to lower spending on content in ‘spiral of decline’ Fewer than half of households in Britain will pay the BBC’s licence within a decade, according to analysis that warns that the broadcaster’s funding is locked in a “spiral of decline” . With senior BBC figures concerned about the accelerating fall in licence fee sales, the independent projections also warn that the proportion of households paying the levy will further decline to less than a third by 2037-38 should the government persist with the corporation’s current funding model. Continue reading...

articles.title: Apple iPhone Duo review: the most novel and interesting iPhone in almost a decade
articles.description: The folding iPhone is early-adopter gold, changing the way iOS works and successfully condensing a tablet into your pocket, but it is not for everyone Apple’s first folding phone has upended the usual order of things with some interesting choices about how you use a iPhone – for better or worse. The Duo sits atop the pile as Apple’s most expensive smartphone – at £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,499) it costs more than most of its folding Android rivals and as much as the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the latest iPad mini combined. Continue reading...

articles.title: Drivers trapped in limbo due to DVLA licence delays
articles.description: It had been revoked on medical grounds but after 12 months I was invited to restore it. Nine months later my application was untouched My driving licence was revoked on medical grounds after I underwent brain surgery for a vascular lesion in 2024. After waiting the required 12 months for my health to stabilise, I was invited to apply for my licence to be restored. I duly sent the evidence from hospital consultants and medical tests. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why I love Berlin in winter: ‘Christmas markets arrive in a blaze of twinkling lights’
articles.description: The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story. Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of twinkling lights, aromatic grill smoke, candied nuts and warming cups of Glühwein. Continue reading...

articles.title: Weird lifestyle advice from Gwyneth Paltrow: best podcasts of the week
articles.description: The Hollywood star is joined by celebrity guests as she shares ‘practical tips’. Plus, David Cameron’s deeply personal series about Alzheimer’s The second podcast from her wellness empire is ostensibly centred on Paltrow’s incredibly niche lifestyle advice: where to eat the “best cacio e pepe in Rome”, for example, or “whether it’s weird to use an obsidian gua sha tool on a plane”. In reality, the show is a weekly cosy chat with a showbiz pal (first up, Zoe Saldaña) peppered with a few practical tips – such as how to eat enough protein if you can’t face any more eggs. Rachel Aroesti Widely available, episodes weekly Continue reading...

articles.title: A taste of Italy: Alessandro Giannatempo’s recipes for Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, and crocodile’s porridge
articles.description: Sweet from top to toe: a creamy, southern Italian fruit and nut cake, and an almondy polenta porridge from the north Although I grew up in Emilia-Romagna, my family history spans the Italian peninsula. Inspired by my mixed upbringing, these recipes reflect the flavours of both southern and northern Italy. The Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, as the name suggests, is a nod to the southern coast of Salerno. Fresh ricotta is whipped with lemony pears and sandwiched between layers of nutty hazelnut cake. The crocodile’s porridge, named after a traditional Italian beverage made with milk and pear juice, combines northern ingredients such as polenta and amaro for a very cosy stovetop-made dessert – or breakfast, if you ask me! Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: Top deck of the bus for the finest views of autumn | John Gilbey
articles.description: Gwynedd: Past golden hillsides and the great Cadair Idris, through wooded valleys, to the starting point for my walk The morning starts bright but cold, with a hazy mist clinging to the trees across the valley. This could be one of the last good weather days, so I take the bus north into Gwynedd, clambering awkwardly upstairs to get the best view of the autumn colours. The mist begins to clear and, in a wet meadow, a heron stands alertly by a ditch, watching for movement. Beyond the Afon Dyfi, the hills are golden with patches of larch and the deeper orange tones of the oak and ash. Well-defined shadows below the dark blue sky shelter pockets of still-frosted gloom, as we cross the Dyfi into Gwynedd. Continue reading...

articles.title: Dapper Liam and Noel, experimental Björk, and Bowie ‘cuddling himself’: Rankin reveals his never-before-seen shots of the stars
articles.description: After some satirical experiments with the ‘disgusting’ AI, the photographer has returned to his first love with a book of contact sheets from his celebrity shoots. ‘I wish we could go back and stop everything changing,’ he says “I hate AI,” says Rankin. “A lot of people think I’m an evangelical twat about it, and I’m not. I think it’s disgusting. I think the people who run it are disgusting. They’ve made a massive gamble with humanity and society and culture.” His contempt may surprise anyone who’s familiar with Rankin’s substantial AI output. Ever since the artist Damien Hirst introduced him to the possibilities of generative AI in 2021, the British photographer has been going further down the rabbit hole. “I’m not somebody who likes to be critical about something without actually knowing about it,” he explains. “I’ve gone deep into trying to work it out.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears
articles.description: Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves Business live – latest updates European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills. The Dutch month-ahead contract – the European benchmark for gas prices over the next four weeks – rose by as much as 8.6% to €96.08, before settling up 4% at €92.50. Continue reading...

articles.title: Is it true that … we only use 10% of our brains?
articles.description: The idea that we access a fraction of our cognitive potential goes back decades, but does medical science agree? This idea really bugs Dr Mary Spiller , senior lecturer in the University of East London’s Department of Psychology and Human Development, who’s shocked by how prevalent it remains, despite being untrue. Spiller says the myth’s origins can partly be traced to the work of William James, one of the founders of modern psychology, working in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He wrote: “We are making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources.” Continue reading...

Thank you, lipstick effect . It can feel like a no-brainer to stock up on our regular favourites and get a few Christmas presents crossed off the list while prices are lower. But deals do something funky to our brains. Retailers know how to lure us in, using big discounts and “selling fast” pop-ups that cause our typically rational brains to short circuit. Add a high-pressure countdown, and before you know it, you’ve been enticed into buying countless products you didn’t set out to buy. articles.title: How freaked out should we be? After mass outages, experts tell us how close we are to ‘doomsday’
articles.description: As tech, travel and banking failures sweep the US, analysts and cyber-security directors discuss AI, underfunding and what keeps them up at night Grounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly. Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure. articles.title: ‘One area of the tent was known as fart corner’: what it’s really like to be on The Great British Bake Off

Like a cloud of Swiss meringue buttercream on a slightly sunken cake, Nigella Lawson has added glamour and indulgence to a format that needed saving. But this year’s contestants have brought the joy, too: talented, charismatic individuals who have interrupted their lives to spend three months with bits of dough stuck to their elbows and indigestion from all the recipe testing. We spoke to five previous contestants to find out why they put themselves through it, and what they feel they achieved in the process. articles.title: Words are not enough after the Myanmar genocide ruling. The world can do better – but it must take these steps | Gordon Brown
articles.description: Atrocities happen again and again. We need a comprehensive framework that would allow us to predict, prevent or respond to them For the first time a state, Myanmar, has been found directly responsible for the crime of genocide . On the instructions of the country’s Tatmadaw regime, at least 10,000 Rohingya men, women and children were murdered, and thousands more were subjected to sexual violence and torture in a 2017 military campaign. While the international court of justice ruled a decade after the crimes that they amounted to genocide, it is unclear whether Myanmar’s leaders will ever be brought to justice, whether any of the more than 1 million Rohingya refugees will be able to return home or whether the country’s government will even have to pay reparations for its crimes. articles.description: The Theranos founder talks in frustrating riddles – but was she lying to us, or to herself? Or could she be a cog in a larger, more sinister, lie-machine? I went to see You Can See Everything with a friend who had never heard of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of blood testing startup Theranos. She knew that she was a convicted fraudster, because as the film opens, Holmes is 34 days from commencing her prison sentence for defrauding investors. But she was completely open-minded as to whether this was definitely fraud or a miscarriage of justice, whether Holmes was the puppeteer or the puppet (of her previous business and romantic partner, Sunny Balwani, who was also convicted of fraud), and whether Holmes’s central claim, of huge diagnostic capabilities from putting a drop of blood into a tiny box, had any scientific foundation. My friend was probably the co-director Nathan Fielder’s perfect viewer, someone who had no preconceptions about what was true: what would she learn, from three hours with a camera so close to the subject’s face that you could count her eyelashes? “Well … She seems nice?” she said after the film had finished. When you’ve got David Cameron, Theresa May, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak saying you’ve got it wrong on Brexit , then the chances are Andy Burnham must be doing something right. These four are the former prime ministers that are largely responsible for the mess the UK is currently in. Lord Big Dave had never really given the possibility of leaving the EU much thought. The Maybot spent three years saying nothing more intelligent than “Brexit means Brexit”. Boris lied through his teeth to get his deal over the line. And as for Rishi? It’s hard to think of anything he achieved. All of which makes life tricky for Kemi Badenoch. Because in an ideal world, Kemi would rather we all forgot about Brexit entirely. articles.title: Will the Jilly Cooper plagiarism allegations taint our love of Rivals? I doubt it | Nadia Khomami
articles.description: The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own. Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”. Nadia Khomami is arts and culture correspondent at the Guardian Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.description: The international court of justice has settled questions over the issue of intent, with powerful implications for Israel The international court of justice (ICJ) decision last Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya recognizes the plight of one of the world’s most persecuted minorities. It also resonates in Gaza, where the same court is now more likely to find that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians. articles.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
articles.description: Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend. Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
articles.description: On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union. Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels. Continue reading...

articles.title: Andy Burnham’s EU deal leaves Brexit open to question | Letters
articles.description: Stuart Finegan says the PM deserves credit for his practical steps to rebuild European relations, while Julian Roberts says the point of democracy is surely the right of the people to change their minds. Plus letters from Lindsay Bray , Helen Elliott and Nick Smith Your article ( Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit, 20 November ) marks a welcome moment of political realism after years of denial about the consequences of Brexit. I wholeheartedly agree with Andy Burnham when he said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe.” For years, the evidence has pointed in the same direction, that the UK economy is worse off as a result of Brexit. Trade barriers have increased, growth has suffered and businesses have been forced to navigate unnecessary bureaucracy. Many of the industries that Brexit supporters claimed would flourish have instead struggled. Fishing, farming, construction and touring musicians have all faced new obstacles, costs and restrictions. Meanwhile, younger generations have seen opportunities to study, work, travel and collaborate across Europe reduced through no fault of their own. The benefits o

articles.title: A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds | Letter
articles.description: Emma Phipps of SongBird Survival writes that the government must act now to save woodland and farmland species from extinction The Office for Environmental Protection’s finding that government departments are breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds should alarm us all ( UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds, 18 November ). The scale of bird declines in the UK is impossible to ignore, and songbirds are among the worst affected. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ wild bird indicators show that nearly 70% of farmland songbird species have declined since 1970. Woodland songbirds are faring little better, with more than 30% of species in decline. Unfortunately, none of this comes as a surprise. Decades of monitoring by scientists and dedicated volunteers have shown that our wild birds are in trouble. Yet successive governments have failed to act with the urgency needed to halt these declines. Continue reading...

articles.title: If Trump, Xi and Putin are carving up the pudding, who gets the sixpence? | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to an article by Rafael Behr on the Shenzhen summit, where the three world leaders met without a place at the table for Europe Rafael Behr ( Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe, 18 November ) draws parallels between the Shenzhen summit and Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin and Franklin D Roosevelt meeting at Yalta. I see it as bringing us a step closer to George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, in which the world is divided into three superstates: Oceania, Eurasia and Eastasia. We already have the surveillance in the form of CCTV, facial-recognition technology and email trawling. Daily we witness the rewriting of history. We could be sleepwalking into a situation from which we will be unable to escape. Andy Fazakerley Irby, Wirral Continue reading...

articles.title: Sweden’s datacentre politics are more complicated than they appear | Letter
articles.description: There are distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources, write James White and Nora Söderberg Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector ( ‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November ) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation. Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign , initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development. Controversy over datacentres in Sweden’s north reflect wider debate about resource extraction for the green and technological transitions, and the worry that Sweden is becoming an “electricity colony” of big tech , providing cheap, green energy while the economic benefits are realised els

articles.description: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . articles.description: Organisers to close top tier of Allianz Stadium on Friday Saturday and Sunday sales stronger with 70% taken The opening night of the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend on Friday is poised to be played in front of around 40,000 empty seats, with the top tier of the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham to be closed. articles.title: Madness erupts as Sevilla deny Betis in wild end to Spain’s ‘derby of derbies’
articles.description: Rivals have been heading in opposite directions in recent years but latest clash showed some things never change “If we didn’t celebrate a goal, especially in this game, that would be madness,” Kike Salas said. Instead, this was madness, the kind of moment a derby is meant to have, even if it has nothing else. It was late, it was lucky, and there wasn’t even a winner but right there, right then, at 24 minutes past 8pm on Saturday evening in the Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán Stadium, it felt like there was. Frankly it was a bit rubbish, as bad a goal as you’ll see, but it was also the best, practically Pelé against the Nazis . Suddenly there were arms and legs everywhere, tears too. Cameras confirmed it. Zoom in and there they are: actual, real life tears. In the 91st minute of the 146th meeting between Sevilla Fútbol Club and Real Betis Balompié – “derby of derbies” according to Luis García, the Sevilla coach for whom it was the first – Salas’s shot from 18 yards went through Marc Bartra’s legs and Álvaro Valles’s hands. The ball dribbled into the Betis net so apologetically it barely touched the net at all and hadn’t got there before Sevilla’s vice-captain was gone. Raised in Morón de la

articles.title: Game over? How playing Grand Theft Auto VI is affecting elite athletes’ performances | Sean Ingle
articles.description: Burning the midnight oil playing video games is not ideal preparation for professional sport – but it’s not all bad “They miss games, the cheque’s still clearing. And you’re trying to tell me they got this kind of addiction to a video game that they sitting there with their thumbs looking like Donald Trump?” That was EPSN’s Stephen A Smith, one of the US’s most provocative and influential sports pundits, spitting fire and fury last week after hearing that so many NBA and NFL stars were absorbed in Grand Theft Auto VI. Smith was hardly an outlier. Other pundits, as well as some Manchester United fans, also questioned Bryan Mbeumo’s focus and professionalism after he posted an image of GTA VI and the word “ historique ” after midnight on Thursday. Meanwhile before last weekend’s Premier League games, the Odd Sport social media account predicted that Chelsea, Brighton and Manchester City would all lose. Why? Because their younger squads might be more focused on Vice City than their opponents, and therefore play with less intensity as a result. By Monday that forecast had been liked tens of thousands of times. Continue reading...

articles.title: Infantino’s $20bn World Cup sell-off plan was to run for up to 96 years, documents show
articles.description: Management team were in line for huge payouts Fifa denies Infantino would have profited from plan Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian. Previously undisclosed communications by Fifa and Thrive Capital, the lead investor for the proposal, cast fresh light on the deal to sell off football’s crown jewels. They outline a plan, produced days before July’s final of the 2026 World Cup, to profit from the sport’s burgeoning commercial revenues for almost a century. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sport of kings will be going to the dogs if horse racing is complacent on welfare
articles.description: Latest greyhound racing blow is a wake-up call with new five-year plan keeping RSPCA on side for now Britain’s greyhound racing industry woke up on Monday to the news that the Racing Post, the daily trade newspaper that has carried extensive coverage of the sport since its launch in 1986, will drop both editorial and greyhound racecards in its print edition from 10 December. In a letter to Racing Post readers, Tom Kerr, its editor, said that it had been an “immensely difficult decision” and blamed “tax rises that have hit betting shops [which] have put pressure on the whole industry,” adding that “like other businesses, we have to make hard choices about where we focus our resources.” Five members of staff are expected to lose their jobs as a result of the decision. articles.title: Inside Fifa and US Soccer’s plan for 2031 World Cup: ‘the largest women’s sporting event in history’
articles.description: The US-led four-country bid was confirmed in Zurich on Monday, projecting record-setting total revenues of $4bn The biggest and most lucrative event in the history of women’s sport was confirmed at an Extraordinary Fifa Congress in Zurich on Monday, with a joint bid from the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031’s Women’s World Cup formally ratified by a vote of Fifa’s 211 member associations. articles.title: Ian Huntley killer felt ‘sick of him’ and that he had nothing to lose, court told
articles.description: Jurors hear inmate Anthony Russell bludgeoned Soham murderer with metal bar after being bullied by him A prisoner thought he had nothing to lose when he killed the Soham murderer, Ian Huntley, by repeatedly striking him over the head with a 4kg iron bar, a court has heard. Anthony Russell, 44, who is serving a whole-life term at HMP Frankland in Durham, told prison staff Huntley had been bullying him and that he had had enough. Continue reading...

articles.description: Ministers proposing to abolish the quangos in attempt to give politicians more control over what gets built and where Scientists have accused the government of scapegoating nature for proposing to scrap the only environmental regulator with a legal duty to protect the natural world. articles.title: From mocked to mainstream: how Spain’s far-right Vox transformed its fortunes
articles.description: Party that won just 0.2% of the vote in 2016 is on course for almost 20% this time and could be part of next government Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain . The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil. Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament.
